name: Python
description: A beginner-friendly language for scripts, data and automation.
setup_check: Run a file containing print("Hello!") and see Hello! printed.

setup_steps.title: Install Python
setup_steps.body: Download Python 3 from python.org and run the installer. On Windows, tick "Add python.exe to PATH" before clicking Install.

setup_steps.title: Check that it works
setup_steps.body: Open a terminal (Command Prompt on Windows, Terminal on Mac) and type python --version (or python3 --version on Mac). You should see a version number.

setup_steps.title: Install a code editor
setup_steps.body: Install Visual Studio Code and add the Python extension from the Extensions panel.

setup_steps.title: Run your first program
setup_steps.body: Make a file called hello.py containing print("Hello!") and run it with python hello.py.

project_ideas.title: Sari-sari store stock counter
project_ideas.brief: Write a program that keeps track of a small store's stock. It asks what was sold, takes it off the count, and warns when an item is running low. By the end it saves the counts to a file so they're still there tomorrow.
done_when: Selling an item lowers its count, and selling more than you have shows a friendly message.
It warns when an item drops below a number you choose.
The counts are saved to a file and loaded the next time it runs.
You can explain each part to a friend.

project_ideas.title: Class survey tally
project_ideas.brief: Write a program that collects answers to one survey question from your class, such as a favourite snack, and counts them. It prints the results from most to least popular.
done_when: It keeps asking for answers until you type done.
It counts answers the same way even with different capitals or extra spaces.
It prints each answer with its count, most popular first.
You can explain each part to a friend.

topics.title: Variables and Data Types
topics.summary: Store values in variables and learn the basic types: int, float, str and bool.
tips: A variable is a name pointing to a value. Use type(x) to see what kind of value x holds.
Text in quotes is a string, even if it looks like a number: "5" + "5" is "55", not 10.

skill_questions.prompt: What is the type of x after this line?

quiz_items.prompt: Write the function that shows the type of a value: ___(42)
quiz_items.hint: It's a built-in that tells you what kind of value you have.

quiz_items.prompt: Turn the text "7" into a whole number: ___("7")
quiz_items.hint: The name of the whole-number type works as a function.

quiz_items.prompt: True and False are values of type ___
quiz_items.hint: Short for Boolean.

practice_tasks.prompt: Make variables for a student: their name (text), age (a whole number), height in meters (a number with a decimal) and whether they're enrolled (True or False). Then print one sentence that uses all four.
practice_tasks.starter_code:
# Make your four variables here


# Print one sentence that uses all four
practice_tasks.sample_answer:
name = "Ana"
age = 19
height = 1.6
enrolled = True

print(name, "is", age, "years old,", height, "m tall. Enrolled:", enrolled)
checklist: Has a str, an int, a float and a bool
Each variable has a clear name
Prints one sentence with all four values
Runs without errors

topics.title: Input and Output
topics.summary: Read what the user types and show results with print and f-strings.
tips: input() always gives you a string. Wrap it in int() or float() if you need a number.
f-strings make output easy: f"Hi {name}!" puts the value of name inside the text.

choices: It depends on what the user types

quiz_items.prompt: Ask the user for their name: name = ___("Name? ")
quiz_items.hint: It's the opposite of print.

quiz_items.prompt: Show a value on the screen: ___("Hello")
quiz_items.hint: You have used this since your first program.

quiz_items.prompt: Put a variable inside text with an f-string: f"Hi ___name}"
quiz_items.hint: Variables in f-strings go inside curly braces.

practice_tasks.prompt: Ask for the user's name and the year they were born. Print a greeting with their name and how old they turn in 2026. Type your test answers in "Input for your program" before pressing Run.
practice_tasks.starter_code:
name = input("What's your name? ")
# Ask for the birth year, then turn it into a number

# Print the greeting
practice_tasks.sample_answer:
name = input("What's your name? ")
born = int(input("What year were you born? "))
age = 2026 - born
print("Hi " + name + "! You turn " + str(age) + " in 2026.")
checklist: Uses input() twice
Turns the year into a number with int()
Works out the age with a calculation
Prints a greeting with the name and age

topics.title: Conditionals
topics.summary: Make decisions with if, elif and else.
tips: Use == to compare and = to assign. if x = 5: is an error; if x == 5: is a check.
Indentation is part of the syntax. Everything indented under if runs only when the condition is true.

skill_questions.prompt: Which keyword checks another condition after if?

quiz_items.prompt: Check another condition: ___ x == 0:
quiz_items.hint: Python shortens "else if" into one word.

quiz_items.prompt: Compare two values for equality: if a ___ b:
quiz_items.hint: One equals sign assigns; you need two.

quiz_items.prompt: Run code when no condition matched: ___:
quiz_items.hint: The catch-all branch.

practice_tasks.prompt: Store a score from 0 to 100 in a variable. Print "Excellent" for 90 and up, "Passed" for 75 to 89, and "Try again" for anything lower. Change the score and run it a few times to check each branch.
practice_tasks.starter_code:
score = 82

# Print Excellent, Passed or Try again
checklist: Uses if, elif and else
The checks go from highest to lowest
Each branch prints the right word
Works for 95, 80 and 50

topics.title: Loops
topics.summary: Repeat code with for and while loops.
tips: range(5) gives 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. It stops before the number you give it.
A while loop needs something inside it that eventually makes the condition false, or it runs forever.

skill_questions.prompt: How many times does this print?
What is the last number printed?

quiz_items.prompt: Loop five times: for i in ___(5):
quiz_items.hint: A built-in that makes a sequence of numbers.

quiz_items.prompt: Stop a loop early: ___
quiz_items.hint: It breaks out of the loop.

quiz_items.prompt: Loop while a condition is true: ___ count < 10:
quiz_items.hint: The other kind of loop besides for.

practice_tasks.prompt: Print the multiplication table of 7, from 7 x 1 to 7 x 10, one line each, like "7 x 3 = 21".
practice_tasks.starter_code:
number = 7

# Use a loop to print 7 x 1 up to 7 x 10
checklist: Uses a for loop with range()
Prints exactly 10 lines
Starts at 1 and ends at 10
Each line shows the right product

topics.title: Lists
topics.summary: Keep many values in order, add to them and loop over them.
tips: List positions start at 0, so the first item is items[0] and the last is items[-1].
append() changes the list in place and returns None, so don't write items = items.append(x).

quiz_items.prompt: Add an item to the end of a list: items.___(5)
quiz_items.hint: A method that attaches to the end.

quiz_items.prompt: Get the last item: items[___]
quiz_items.hint: Negative positions count from the end.

quiz_items.prompt: Count the items in a list: ___(items)
quiz_items.hint: Short for length.

practice_tasks.prompt: Make a list of five prices. Add one more with append(). Then print the cheapest price, the most expensive, and the total.
practice_tasks.starter_code:
prices = [120, 45, 300, 80, 55]

# Add one more price

# Print the cheapest, the most expensive and the total
practice_tasks.sample_answer:
prices = [120, 45, 300, 80, 55]
prices.append(99)

print("Cheapest:", min(prices))
print("Most expensive:", max(prices))
print("Total:", sum(prices))
checklist: Adds a price with append()
Finds the cheapest and most expensive
Prints the total
Prints labels so the numbers make sense

topics.title: Functions
topics.summary: Package code into reusable functions with parameters and return values.
tips: print shows a value; return hands it back to whoever called the function. They are not the same.
A function without a return statement returns None.

quiz_items.prompt: Start a function definition: ___ greet(name):
quiz_items.hint: Short for define.

quiz_items.prompt: Send a value back from a function: ___ total
quiz_items.hint: It ends the function and gives back a value.

quiz_items.prompt: A function with no return gives back ___
quiz_items.hint: Python's value for "nothing". Capital N.

practice_tasks.prompt: Write a function average(numbers) that returns the average of a list of numbers. Call it on two different lists and print both results.
practice_tasks.starter_code:
def average(numbers):
    # Return the average
    pass


print(average([80, 90, 70]))
checklist: Defines average with one parameter
Uses return, not print, inside the function
Is called on two different lists

topics.title: Dictionaries
topics.summary: Store values by key, look them up and loop over them.
tips: Use d.get(key) when the key might be missing; d[key] raises KeyError instead.
Loop over d.items() to get each key and value together.

quiz_items.prompt: Get each key and value in a loop: for k, v in d.___():
quiz_items.hint: It gives pairs.

quiz_items.prompt: Look up a key without an error if it's missing: d.___("name")
quiz_items.hint: A safe way to read a value.

quiz_items.prompt: Check if a key exists: if "name" ___ d:
quiz_items.hint: The same word you use in for loops.

practice_tasks.prompt: Make a dictionary of three friends and their favorite food. Add a fourth friend, then loop through the dictionary and print "Name likes food" for each one.
checklist: Adds a new key and value
Loops with .items()
Prints one line per friend
Prints four lines

topics.title: Working with Files and Handling Exceptions
topics.summary: Read and write files, and handle errors with try and except.
tips: Open files with with open(...) as f: so Python closes them for you, even if an error happens.
Catch specific errors like ValueError instead of a bare except:, so real bugs aren't hidden.

skill_questions.prompt: Which mode opens a file for reading?

quiz_items.prompt: Start a block that might fail: ___:
quiz_items.hint: You try something, then catch errors.

quiz_items.prompt: Handle the error: ___ ValueError:
quiz_items.hint: Python's word for catch.

quiz_items.prompt: Open a file so it closes itself: ___ open("a.txt") as f:
quiz_items.hint: A context manager keyword.

practice_tasks.prompt: Ask for a number and print its double. If the user types something that isn't a number, print "That's not a number" instead of crashing. Test it with "5" and with "hello" in the input box.
practice_tasks.starter_code:
text = input("Type a number: ")

# Use try and except to handle text that isn't a number
checklist: Uses try and except
Catches ValueError
Prints the double for a number
Prints a friendly message for text
